piezas.titulo: Cortical responses to lipread and text-based audiovisual stimuli in adults with and without dyslexia
piezas.resumenOriginal: Phonetic recalibration enables listeners to adjust their perception of ambiguous speech sounds based on visual contextual information. In line with a specific difficulty in forming letter-speech sound associations, adults with dyslexia have been found to show no text-based, but intact lipread-based, recalibration. The underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear however. This fMRI study examined cortical responses during text-based and lipread-based phonetic recalibration in 34 adults (18 with dyslexia, 16 typical readers). Participants were exposed to ambiguous speech sounds /a?a/ paired with disambiguating visual information (“aba”/“ada” text or lipread videos), followed by auditory-only categorization trials. Contrary to previous findings, both groups showed robust text-based and lipread-based behavioral recalibration effects, with no significant group differences between typical and dyslexic readers. Neuroimaging data did yield group differences in the underlying cortical activation. Most notably, dyslexic readers demonstrated increased bilateral fusiform activation compared to typical readers during exposure to lipread videos and ambiguous speech sounds, with left fusiform activation specifically correlating with increased phonological processing difficulties. Additionally, typical readers exhibited higher right frontal activation during text-based audiovisual stimuli. These findings suggest that while adults with dyslexia did not differ significantly from typical readers in behavioral recalibration effects, they employed different neural processing strategies. Unexpectedly, this was particularly the case for lipread audiovisual stimuli. The relatively increased fusiform and superior temporal activation to lipread audiovisual stimuli in dyslexic readers possibly relates to subtle difficulties in phonological processing of ambiguous speech signals.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede la visión compensar la dislexia? piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: Somatosensory phenotyping in women with persistent genital arousal disorder: a case-control study.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Introduction Persistent genital arousal disorder (PGAD) is a rare and distressing condition characterized by persistent, unwanted genital arousal in the absence of sexual desire or stimulation. Persistent genital arousal disorder is increasingly recognized as a disorder of abnormal genital sensory processing, but objective neurophysiological data remain limited. Methods We conducted an exploratory case-control study to characterize somatosensory function in women with PGAD. Thirty women with PGAD and 30 age-matched healthy controls were recruited at Leiden University Medical Center. Participants underwent quantitative sensory testing (QST) at hand and external genital sites, conditioned pain modulation, and corneal confocal microscopy. Results Hand QST values were within normal range in both groups. In the genital region, PGAD participants showed altered thermal pain processing, with cold and heat hyperalgesia compared with controls. Mechanical pain thresholds did not differ between groups; however, PGAD participants reported higher pain intensity ratings to mechanical stimuli and showed significantly greater temporal summation of pain in genital regions. Genital dynamic mechanical allodynia occurred more frequently in PGAD participants but did not differ significantly at the group level. Conditioned pain modulation magnitude did not differ between groups and showed substantial interindividual variability. Corneal confocal microscopy abnormalities were observed in a proportion of participants in both groups without significant between-group differences. Discussion These findings show that QST is feasible in women with PGAD and indicate that PGAD is associated with altered somatosensory processing demonstrating genital thermal hypersensitivity and central pain sensitization in a subset of patients.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades): T.A.C.T is a 501(c)(3) that provides trade and technical skills to children, young adults and families living with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. About Developmental Pathways: Developmental Pathways is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit agency serving individuals with developmental disabilities/delays and their families. We are also one of Colorado’s Community Centered Boards (CCB) connecting people to federal, state, county, and private funding in Arapahoe County, Douglas County, and the City of Aurora. We passionately believe inclusion is for everyone and offer services through Home and Community Based Medicaid Waiver programs, locally funded programs, and partnerships with other community organizations. piezas.titulo: A brief neuromotor-therapy-augmented pathway for pediatric functional movement disorders: a sequential historical cohort study
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundPediatric functional movement disorders (FMD) often improve, but access to specialized motor rehabilitation is heterogeneous. We compared two sequential, non-overlapping care periods within one clinical unit: usual care (UC) and a neuromotor-therapy-augmented pathway (NMT-A), which added brief hospital-based neuromotor therapy before community referral.MethodsThis retrospective, non-randomized historical cohort included 17 UC patients (June 2021–January 2023) and 29 NMT-A patients (February 2023–June 2025). The primary outcome was continuous S-FMDRS at 6 months; S-FMDRS-defined motor symptom-free status (score = 0) was secondary. Both were reassessed at 12 months, together with community-treatment engagement.ResultsAt 6 months, the adjusted NMT-A-minus-UC S-FMDRS difference was −1.66 points (95% CI, −4.04 to 0.72). Motor symptom-free status occurred in 55.2% versus 5.9% (risk difference, 49.3 percentage points; 95% CI, 21.8 to 66.4), and in 86.2% versus 52.9% at 12 months (risk difference, 33.3 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.5 to 56.8). The pathway-by-time interaction was not significant. Sustained community physical and/or occupational therapy was documented in 75.0% versus 17.6% (RR, 4.25; 95% CI, 1.74–12.46).ConclusionThe NMT-A pathway-period was associated with more frequent motor symptom-free status and greater continuity of community motor rehabilitation, although the adjusted mean S-FMDRS difference was not statistically significant. Because pathway and calendar period were inseparable, these findings should be interpreted as associations with the overall later care pathway rather than as an isolated effect of NMT.

piezas.titulo: Characterizing Recoverable Expert-Utilization Signatures in Fine-Tuned Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.41039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules. We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.

piezas.titulo: HERC1 Loss of Function Causes a Developmental Disorder with Impaired Hippocampal Function
piezas.resumenOriginal: Pathogenic variants in HERC1 are associated with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by macrocephaly, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and psychomotor dysfunction. Although genetic and molecular studies suggest a loss-of-function mechanism, definitive in vivo evidence that HERC1 deficiency is sufficient to cause neurodevelopmental abnormalities is lacking. Using a HERC1 knockout mouse model, we investigated the behavioural, neuronal, and synaptic consequences of complete HERC1 loss. HERC1 deficiency caused motor coordination and cognitive deficits in both sexes, while male mutants additionally displayed hyperactivity and increased anxiety-like behaviour. Histological analyses revealed selective hippocampal abnormalities, including disruption of dentate gyrus organization, whereas Purkinje cells survival and cerebellar compartmentalization remained preserved. HERC1-deficient mice exhibited a marked increase in hippocampal GABAergic interneurons, impaired maturation of dendritic spines in CA1 pyramidal neurons, and altered adult neurogenesis, indicating widespread defects in hippocampal circuit organization. Consistent with these structural abnormalities, glutamatergic synaptic components were significantly altered throughout the hippocampus. These molecular changes showed a sex-dependent pattern, with predominantly presynaptic defects in males and postsynaptic alterations in females. Despite these differences, whole-cell recordings revealed a common functional phenotype in both sexes. At both mossy fibre-CA3 and Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses, HERC1-deficient neurons exhibited a progressive inability to sustain excitatory neurotransmission during repetitive stimulation, resulting in impaired steady-state glutamatergic transmission. Together, these findings demonstrate that loss of HERC1 function is sufficient to produce a neurodevelopmental phenotype and identify HERC1 as a critical regulator of hippocampal circuit assembly and function. Our results provide mechanistic insight into the pathogenesis of HERC1-associated disorders and establish the Herc1 knockout mouse as a preclinically relevant model for investigating disease mechanisms and therapeutic approaches.

piezas.titulo: Imaging findings and clinical outcomes in neonates with isolated subependymal echogenicity on cranial ultrasound: a retrospective cohort study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo describe clinical and imaging findings in neonates with isolated subependymal echogenicity on cranial ultrasound and examine associations with recorded mortality and cerebral palsy.MethodsThis retrospective single-center cohort included 317 neonates admitted between January 2015 and December 2018 with an initial ultrasound finding suspicious for isolated subependymal hemorrhage. Clinical records, available MRI findings, and follow-up information were reviewed. Cerebral palsy was ascertained from rehabilitation or neurology diagnostic records, supplemented by telephone follow-up in January 2026, independently of developmental test scores. The primary adjusted analysis compared death with all survivors using an exploratory six-item comorbidity count and clinical covariates; hospitalization duration was excluded, and laterality was coded as unilateral or bilateral.ResultsThere were 52 deaths (16.4%), 9 survivors with recorded cerebral palsy (2.8%), and 256 survivors without recorded cerebral palsy (80.8%). MRI findings were compatible with hemorrhage in 61 of 90 examined infants (67.8%). In the complete-case mortality model (n = 316), each additional comorbidity was associated with greater odds of death (adjusted OR, 2.462; 95% CI, 1.787–3.391; p < 0.001). The other included covariates were not statistically significant. White matter abnormalities were recorded in nine infants, including eight of the nine infants with cerebral palsy and one without recorded cerebral palsy.ConclusionSystemic comorbidity burden was associated with mortality within this ultrasound-defined cohort. White matter abnormalities accompanied most recorded cerebral palsy cases, but this observation remains descriptive. Specialist diagnostic records and later telephone follow-up characterize persistent clinical diagnoses; they do not establish the independent effect of subependymal echogenicity or normal development across all domains in survivors without cerebral palsy.

piezas.resumenOriginal:
This is the first of a two-part series exploring how Google Cloud is bringing the foundational values of a high-performance parallel filesystem–TB/s throughput, sub-ms latency at high client scale, and POSIX support–to a broader set of use cases and users. Historically, due to the cost and special purpose nature of parallel filesystems, colder data had to be stored outside of the filesystem and AI developers have had to maintain separate, slower environments for writing code, compiling libraries, and managing repositories. This fragmentation increases the toil of manual data staging, dataset copying, and managing disjointed namespaces. Google Cloud Managed Lustre is solving these problems through our 6 cents/GB*month Dynamic Tier and by optimizing Managed Lustre performance for a range of development tasks and workloads – making Managed Lustre a “One-Stop Shop” for high-performance AI and HPC workloads. Lower Cost: More Lustre for Less with the Dynamic Tier The Managed Lustre Dynamic Tier provides sub-ms latency for hot data, which allows you to store all of your data in a single namespace, and costs only 6 cents/GB*month . Throughput, capacity scale and client scale: Throughput scales linearly with capacity up to 80 PB, while sub-ms latency for hot data remains stable as you scale to tens of thousands of clients. Single-flat fee: Predictable pricing. No independent charges for disk media types, data movement within the namespace, or metadata IOPS. Read Latencies: Sub-ms latencies for High-Performance Cache (SSD). The Capacity Pool (“HDD”) is built on Google Cloud Hyperdisk throughput, which has an average read latency of 10 to 30 ms . Recommended workloads for Dynamic Tier Multi-Epoch Training and/or Training with Optimized Fetch Sizes: Hot data is promoted to the High Performance Cache (SSD) after the first run. Larger data prefetch will allow you to take advantage of the Dynamic Tier cost structure and gain from low-latency SSD. Write-Heavy Checkpointing: Bursty checkpoint writes land directly in the High Performance Cache. Older checkpoints are transparently demoted to the Capacity Pool (HDD). Rapid Checkpoint Restore: New checkpoints are written to the High Performance Cache, enabling low-latency checkpoint restores. Interactive Snappiness for Developers: Low-latency tasks like git cloning, compiling libraries, or running notebooks benefit from a local-disk feel (~300µs average read latencies) on the same shared workspace hosting large training sets. Frictionless development: Lustre as a one-stop shop for developer’s workloads In addition to Managed Lustre’s scalability for large AI and HPC workloads (checkpoint/restart/data-loading), it also meets the demands for interactive work, meaning developers can start on Managed Lustre and stay on Managed Lustre throughout the entire workload lifecycle: Unified Foundation & Interactive Performance Consolidates the AI and HPC lifecycle into a single namespace, providing a "local disk" feel for interactive work (Read more about the latency benefits of Managed Lustre experienced by Salesforce and others ). Latency: ~300µs average read latency—delivering up to 4x better responsiveness than alternative distributed file systems. Accelerated Setup: Untar the Linux kernel in ~2 minutes (4.7x faster than alternative file solutions), run a 20-worker parallel git clone of Python in ~40 seconds, compile Python in ~200s. High-Concurrency Broadcast & Cluster Startup Managed Lustre maximizes GPU ROI by preventing storage bottlenecks during cluster initialization. When thousands of worker nodes attempt to read the exact same file simultaneously (such as a shared model checkpoint, base weights, or container layer), traditional distributed file systems can choke on localized hotspotting, leaving high-cost GPU clusters idle for minutes. piezas.titulo: ROSTrans: Empirically Benchmarking LLMs for ROS1-to-ROS2 Migration
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.41168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although large language models have shown strong capabilities in domain-specific code generation, their performance in robotics software development, especially for the Robot Operating System (ROS), remains largely unexplored. ROS code generation presents distinctive challenges, including complex inter-node coordination, middleware configuration, and lifecycle semantics that go far beyond standard coding benchmarks, and many important correctness properties become observable only once migrated nodes are launched and communicate. We present ROSTrans, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on ROS1-to-ROS2 code migration, a representative and practically important setting for ROS code generation. ROSTrans comprises 108 scaffolded completion tasks drawn from a diverse set of 70+ open-source ROS1 repositories and organized into a hierarchical taxonomy assessing interface-level, behavioral-level and system-level correctness. For every task we establish an executable reference: a verified ROS2 implementation, a runtime test suite that launches the nodes and exercises their topics, services, actions and parameters, and a container ensuring reproducibility. Candidates are scored by injecting only their target files into an otherwise fixed copy of the reference package, so a candidate can neither supply nor weaken the tests it is judged by. Evaluating six frontier LLMs over five stochastic generations per task, we find pass@1 below 10.9%, and that 56.5% of all samples build successfully and then fail at runtime,and 32.0% fail runtime assertions on the migrated interfaces, a class of error no compile-only oracle can detect. Execution-guided repair further improves task success, reaching 49.1% and 47.2% for Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5 after three rounds, respectively.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: September 16
piezas.resumenOriginal: Reports of agentic hacking continue, in this case it happened back in May and it seems OpenAI did not disclose that they were responsible. Simon Willison sees two options: After the Hugging Face and Wiki attacks OpenAI were still unable to review their previous logs and determine that they had previously attacked RubyGems. They knew about the attack on RubyGems and made the decision not to reach out to the RubyGems team about it. Both of these are bad! Given this incident, the Hugging Face situation, and the Wiki attack, the obvious question right now is how many more incidents like this are out there waiting to be discovered? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Dave Farley: Stop asking the sci-fi question: ‘Is it conscious?’ Start asking the engineering question: ‘Is this a powerful, unpredictable component being put somewhere consequential, and where’s the feedback that tells us that it’s safe? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Nate Silver is known for his forecasts, but to do them he writes a lot of code for his models. He’s found agentic engineering capable of doing miraculous work . In spending so much time with the LLMs, I’m super attentive to improvements in their capabilities. And these changes tend not to be so linear. Instead, they improve in step functions, almost as phase changes. Suddenly, the models just start doing things capably that they were screwing up before. In my experience, there was a big leap forward when reasoning models first came out in late 2024/early 2025 — enough that they were occasionally useful for tasks involving data and not just words — and then another one this past winter. The most recent changes I’ve noticed, however, have had less to do with intelligence and more with persistence. Consider the Hugging Face attack. Although these agents showed remarkable intelligence, they weren’t really super-intelligent - but they were super-persistent. This is a common theme of AI in its various forms: Game engines like AlphaGo Zero start out by basically making random moves — but by playing against themselves millions of times, they eventually far surpass human capabilities As we try to figure out what kind of regulations we need to keep AI under control, we need to remember that we should design our guards around super-persistence as much as worrying about super-intelligence. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ “Uncle Bob” Martin has made many posts on X during the last few months about his programming with LLMs. His approach has been to build a firm harness to keep them under control, so they create software that is maintainable as well as functional. Sadly the posts have been frustratingly light on detail. But now it seems that lack of information may not matter And while I was heads-down getting that to work, the agents got a LOT better. So much so that when I came up for air, the need for my harness was obviated. Indeed, the need for any but the most liberal of harnesses may be obviated. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Some tidbits that struck me from Ezra Klein’s recent (recommended) interview with Matt Sheehan on the interplay between regulation of AI and competition with China . While Chinese models have made some surprisingly remarkable gains in the slipstream of US frontier models, the US still has 8 times as much compute available to it than China - which is a material gap. People in the US worry that regulation will slow down the US model builders, but these rapid recent gains in China have occurred under much more regulation Americans say that when they set up a hotline to talk to Chinese leaders in a crisis, the Chinese don’t pick up the phone. But this misunderstands the Chinese system. Individual Chinese, even powerful ones, aren’t given individual decision-making power. They operate with committees and documents. So the Americans are better off sending a fax than trying to call an individual Like so many things, effective regulation needs regular practice When American policymakers are like: Where do you start? — I sometimes say: Well, you start by starting. You learn how to regulate things, you learn how to legislate on them by regulating and legislating on them.

piezas.titulo: How Top-Down Are We? Reconsidering the Gap Between Occupational Therapy's Identity and Practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Occupational therapy has spent more than a century defining occupation as its professional core. Yet studies across countries and settings show a recurring gap. Therapists value occupation-centered practice while often relying on impairment-focused assessment and intervention. This article argues that the profession may face a translation problem more than an identity problem. Biomedical service structures, standardized measurement, workplace culture, and professional socialization can pull reasoning toward body functions. Bottom-up methods are not inherently incompatible with occupational therapy; the problem arises when change in a component is treated as sufficient evidence of occupational success. Drawing on occupational therapy research, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, rehabilitation science, and disability rights, we argue that occupation and participation should remain the outcomes that organize assessment, intervention, and evaluation. Practical changes are proposed for clinical reasoning, outcome measurement, education, supervision, and service design.

piezas.titulo: Altered stimulus-intensity encoding occurs in the primary somatosensory cortex of a central post-stroke pain rat model.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Central post-stroke pain (CPSP) is a chronic form of pain that develops after ventral posterolateral thalamus (VPL) lesions and may involve maladaptive plasticity within central somatosensory pathways. Although abnormalities in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are observed in patients and animal models, the mechanism by which thalamic lesions alter cortical processing of sensory stimuli remains unclear. Here, we investigated stimulus intensity encoding and dendritic remodeling in S1 using a VPL-lesion CPSP rat model. Behavioral assessments were conducted, and mechanical allodynia was observed 3 weeks after lesion induction. Accordingly, the animals were examined during the early (1 week) and late (4-5 weeks) phases after VPL lesions. A distorted stimulus-response relationship was observed in S1 during the late phase, as indicated from voltage-sensitive dye imaging. The responses to low-intensity stimuli were enhanced, and response scaling at higher stimulus intensities was reduced. Increased cortical sensitivity to weak stimuli was associated with the severity of mechanical allodynia. Additionally, morphological analyses were conducted on layer II/III pyramidal neurons. Distinct patterns of dendritic remodeling were observed. Apical dendritic length and branching diminished during the early phase, while basal dendritic arborization increased during the late phase. These findings suggest that time-dependent structural and functional reorganization occurs in S1 following thalamic injury. This reorganization may contribute to abnormal sensory processing in patients with CPSP and offer new insights into the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms.

piezas.titulo: Occupational therapy interventions for functional neurological disorder: a scoping review
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionFunctional Neurological Disorder (FND) is a common and disabling condition for which multidisciplinary rehabilitation is recommended; however, the specific contribution of occupational therapy remains poorly defined. This scoping review aimed to map and characterize occupational therapy interventions for people with FND, examine how these are delivered and evaluated within rehabilitation and identify priorities for future research.MethodsA scoping review was conducted using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology. Peer-reviewed English-language intervention studies involving adults (≥18 years) with FND who received occupational therapy delivered independently or as part of multidisciplinary rehabilitation and reporting treatment outcomes were included. Descriptive analysis was undertaken. OVID Medline, Embase, APA PsycInfo and CINAHL Plus were searched from inception to July 2026, supplemented by reference list screening.ResultsForty-one studies (n= 1,284 participants; sample sizes 1–201) were included, with only one randomized study. Occupational therapy was predominantly delivered within multidisciplinary rehabilitation; only one study included a subgroup receiving occupational therapy alone. Despite considerable variation in intervention reporting, common occupational therapy intervention components included facilitating occupational engagement, movement retraining and anxiety management, with symptom management strategies integrated into functional activities to promote confidence and independence. Improvements in symptom severity, functional ability, mental health, and quality of life were reported following multidisciplinary rehabilitation including occupational therapy. However, findings were primarily derived from uncontrolled studies, and interpretation was further limited by heterogeneity in intervention approaches, inconsistent use of outcome measures, and variable follow-up.DiscussionAlthough occupational therapy was included in all eligible studies, occupational therapy-specific interventions and associated outcomes were inconsistently described and evaluated, limiting understanding of occupational therapy's distinct contribution within multidisciplinary rehabilitation. Future research should focus on clearly defining and evaluating the components of occupational therapy interventions.

piezas.titulo: Recurrent Spiking Neural Networks for Continuous Motor Control: A Biologically Plausible Model of Motor Cortex
piezas.resumenOriginal: Motor cortex acquires skilled movements through recurrent spiking dynamics and experience-dependent synaptic plasticity, yet how such circuits learn continuous motor control using biologically local signals remains unclear. Here, we develop a recurrent spiking neural network model of motor cortex that addresses both the computational and biological requirements of motor learning. We first analytically derived the recurrent firing-rate state directly from synaptic input and trained the network by implicit differentiation, thereby avoiding backpropagation through long spike trajectories. We then introduced State-Carry Initialization, which enables closed-loop motor control by continuously carrying the ongoing recurrent state across successive actions. Building on this formulation, we devised a learning rule termed Feedback-Spike Nudging (FSN), in which teaching signals are delivered as spikes through a feedback pathway. Synaptic changes depend only on presynaptic activity and the feedback-evoked change in postsynaptic firing, consistent with biological mechanisms of synaptic plasticity in motor cortex. The resulting networks learned continuous motor control through both supervised and reinforcement learning, which could be mapped respectively onto interactions of motor cortex with the cerebellum and basal ganglia. Moreover, the FSN learning rule was consistent with experimental observations of structural spine plasticity in mouse motor cortex. Thus, our study lays a foundation for recurrent spiking models of motor cortex that are biologically grounded at both the functional and anatomical levels.

piezas.titulo: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
piezas.resumenOriginal: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

piezas.titulo: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
piezas.resumenOriginal: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. piezas.titulo: Prefrontal cortical morphometric covariance and cognitive task performance in healthy young adults: an exploratory analysis of Human Connectome Project data
piezas.resumenOriginal: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is implicated in many cognitive tasks, including working memory, reward-based decision-making, executive control, and metacognition. This exploratory analysis investigated whether individual expression of PFC cortical thickness and surface area covariance components is associated with cognitive task performance. The sample comprised Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data from 743 healthy adults (age 22–36+). Oblimin-rotated principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to residualized thickness and surface area for 22 PFC regions, controlling for age, sex, and ICV. Component scores were entered as predictors in separate regression models for the Flanker Age-Adjusted Score (inhibitory control), the Gambling RT Difference (RT for the same “larger” guess in reward minus punishment blocks), and 2-Back median RT (working memory speed). Parallel analysis favored two thickness components; a prespecified three-component solution (Global/Lateral PFC, RC1; Orbitofrontal, RC2; Anterior Cingulate, RC3; 53.7% of variance) was retained by decision, and RC1 and RC2 were only moderately stable across bootstrap resamples. RC1 was nominally associated with lower Flanker scores (β = −0.103, p = 0.027), opposite to the predicted direction, and RC2 with a smaller Gambling RT Difference (β = −0.103, p = 0.025); neither survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q = 0.054). In uncorrected models added at review, whole-cortex mean thickness alone robustly predicted Flanker scores but not the Gambling RT Difference; neither component association survived regressing mean thickness out before PCA. In surface area analyses, greater orbitofrontal surface area (AC2) was associated with faster 2-Back RT (β = −0.125, p = 0.003; q = 0.032 across 12 surface area tests and 0.064 across all 24 component tests), not explained by a speed-accuracy tradeoff. This unpredicted association persisted in most sensitivity analyses but was attenuated and non-significant when total surface area was regressed out before PCA (β = −0.065, p = 0.078). In conclusion, no prefrontal-specific association was robust. Global cortical thickness accounts for the Flanker association more parsimoniously, the Gambling RT Difference association was not robust under either account, and the orbitofrontal surface area association could not be separated from global surface area; all associations require replication.

destilado.texto: No es solo que la corteza prefrontal sea más gruesa: su superficie también parece afectar la velocidad de la memoria de trabajo. Un estudio exploratorio del Human Connectome Project con 743 jóvenes sugiere que mayor área orbitofrontal acelera el 2‑Back, aunque la asociación no supera la corrección estadística.

piezas.titulo: Lifestyle Documentation in Therapy Evaluations for Autistic Children: A Lexicon-Based Analysis of Electronic Health Records.
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundWhole person health (WPH) is a multidimensional construct encompassing, physical, and mental health along with relational constructs such as social health that are deeply tied to well-being. Autistic individuals report an overall lower quality of life, but the extent to which these issues are addressed during therapy evaluations has not been examined systematically.MethodologyIn this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we employ a rule-based NLP/lexicon-based approach to examine the areas of focus of therapy evaluations documented by occupational therapy, physical therapy (PT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) professionals. Using electronic health records for children aged 2 to 18 diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (n = 5619 evaluation reports of n = 2021 unique patients), we classified health records based on the domains addressed.ResultsAcross notes, nutrition had the highest average degree of documentation ( M = 2.14), compared to activity ( M = 0.91), followed by wellness ( M = 0.66), and sleep ( M = 0.39). In occupational therapy, wellness was the most common (77.62% of notes), followed by physical activity (76.49% of notes), nutrition management (73.33% of notes), and sleep (34.97% of notes). The overall area under the curve (AUC) from the receiver operating characteristic analysis is 0.89.ConclusionsWhile it is encouraging that most evaluations addressed nutrition or physical activity, the near absence of attention to sleep represents a critical gap in care. Given sleep's foundational role in overall health and daily functioning, its omission is particularly concerning. Occupational therapists and interdisciplinary rehabilitation teams should more deliberately integrate WPH frameworks into their evaluations.

piezas.titulo: Effects of primary somatosensory cortex high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation combined with core stability training on pain and glutamate levels and neuromuscular function in chronic low back pain: a randomized controlled trial.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Chronic low back pain (CLBP) involves pain-related changes in sensory processing, motor control, and broader neurobiological function. The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is a relevant neuromodulation target because it contributes to sensory-discriminative pain processing and exhibits maladaptive plasticity in chronic pain states. However, S1-targeted high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) has been insufficiently studied in CLBP. Objective To determine whether S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training reduces pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP, and to explore associated changes in paraspinal muscle biomechanical properties, resting-state EEG activity, and serum metabolites. Methods In this randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 36 adults with CLBP received active or sham S1 HD-tDCS combined with a standardized 4-week core stability training program. Pain-related scale was assessed using the VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ. Secondary outcomes included biomechanical properties of the lumbar erector spinae and multifidus measured using MyotonPRO. Exploratory outcomes included resting-state electroencephalographic alpha-band power spectral density (PSD) and phase-locking value (PLV) connectivity, as well as untargeted serum metabolomics in a subset of participants. Results Compared with sham stimulation, active S1 HD-tDCS was associated with greater reductions in VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ scores after treatment. The active group also showed larger decreases in lumbar erector spinae and multifidus tone and stiffness, along with greater improvement in elasticity. Resting-state EEG demonstrated increased alpha-band PSD across frontal, central, and parieto-occipital regions and reduced alpha-band PLV connectivity after active stimulation. In the metabolomics subset, active treatment was associated with greater reductions in circulating L-glutamate and enrichment of ferroptosis-related pathways. Changes in pain intensity were correlated with changes in paraspinal muscle stiffness, central alpha-band PSD, and L-glutamate levels. Conclusions S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training may improve short-term pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP. The accompanying muscular, electrophysiological, and metabolomic findings were consistent with the clinical changes. These findings support S1-targeted HD-tDCS as a potential adjunct to exercise-based rehabilitation in CLBP. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300076620 (Registration date 2023-10-13).
